## Beyond Probability, RVs, and Expectation {.smaller}

Now we also want to know:

::: {.incremental}
-   What's the chance that something lies between particular values?
    -   e.g. polyarchy score — does it exceed 0.5?
    -   Sum up infinitely small pieces and integrate!
-   At particular values of any RV, how does the chance — the probability — change?
    -   Differentiate the distribution / PDF to find out.
:::

## Today {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   **First, what the tools are for** — learn to *read* $\int$, $\lim$, and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$: integration as area under a curve, limits as the shrinking move underneath it, differentiation as change at a point.
-   **Then, how to compute them** — in the order the math builds: limits → derivatives → integrals.
    -   Saving integration's mechanics for last is what makes the antiderivative a one-line observation instead of a mystery.
-   **The Join** — deriving bivariate $\hat\beta$ from a minimization criterion.
:::

## Refresher: PMF, PDF, Expectation {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%" style="font-size:0.6em;"}
-   **PMF** — discrete $X$: $p(x) = P(X = x)$; each bar's *height* is a probability.
    -   $p(x) \ge 0$ and $\displaystyle\sum_x p(x) = 1$.
-   **PDF** — continuous $X$: heights are *densities*; only **areas** are probabilities.
    -   $f(x) \ge 0$, $\;\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1$, $\;P(a \le X \le b) = \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
-   **Expectation** — the probability-weighted average: the distribution's balance point.
    -   Discrete: $E[X] = \displaystyle\sum_x x\,p(x)$.
    -   Continuous: $E[X] = \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,f(x)\,dx$ — $\int$ replaces $\sum$, $f(x)\,dx$ replaces $p(x)$.
:::

## Integration & Area Under the Curve

*Where probability lives for continuous variables: the area under a curve.*

## Why We Need It {.smaller}

```{=html}

    <text x="197" y="184" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2f855a">4</text>
    <text x="425" y="184" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5A6B80">10</text>
    <path d="M197,45 L197,32" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="1.5"/>

  </g>
</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.incremental}
-   Binomial($n=10$, $p=0.5$): 10 coin flips, $k$ = number of heads.
    -   PMF: $P(X=k) = \binom{10}{k}(0.5)^{10}$ — one bar per possible outcome.
    -   $P(X=4) = \binom{10}{4}(0.5)^{10} = \dfrac{210}{1024} \approx 0.205$ — read straight off the bar.
:::

## The Same Toolkit, Concretely {.smaller}

Every PMF/CDF/$E[X]$ we've used is a finite sum, $\Sigma$, over the bars above.

::: {.incremental}
-   PMF: $\sum_{k=0}^{10} p(k) = 1$ — all eleven bars add to 1.
-   CDF: $F(4) = \sum_{k=0}^{4} p(k) = \dfrac{1+10+45+120+210}{1024} \approx 0.377$.
-   $E[X] = \sum_{k=0}^{10} k\,p(k) = 10(0.5) = 5$.
:::


::: {.incremental}
-   No bars here — $f(x)$ is a curve, and $P(X=x)=0$ at any single point.
    -   "What's the chance $X$ is between $a$ and $b$?" is the shaded area under $f(x)$.
-   There's no list of bars left to add — we need a way to sum the area under a curve.
    -   That's what integration is for.
:::

## Density vs. Probability {.smaller}

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; margin: 4px 0 4px;">
<svg width="470" height="205" viewBox="0 0 470 205" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <text x="100" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303F">A Single Point</text>
  <text x="350" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303F">A Tiny Interval</text>
  <g transform="translate(0,15)">
    <g>
      <path d="M10,120 Q100,-80 190,120" fill="none" stroke="#22303F" stroke-width="2"/>
      <line x1="10" y1="120" x2="190" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <line x1="100" y1="120" x2="100" y2="20" stroke="#B23A48" stroke-width="2.5"/>
      <text x="12" y="45" font-size="12" font-style="italic" fill="#22303F">PDF f(x)</text>
      <text x="100" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#B23A48">width → 0</text>
      <text x="100" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#B23A48">P(X=x₀) = 0</text>
    </g>
    <g transform="translate(250,0)">
      <path d="M10,120 Q100,-80 190,120" fill="none" stroke="#22303F" stroke-width="2"/>
      <line x1="10" y1="120" x2="190" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <rect x="130" y="45" width="20" height="75" fill="#38a169" fill-opacity="0.4" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="100" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2f855a">width = dx</text>
      <text x="100" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2f855a">≈ f(x₁)·dx</text>
    </g>
  </g>
</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.incremental}
-   Why the split? A discrete RV has **countably many** values — probability can sit on each one as a positive mass and still sum to $1$.
    -   A continuous RV has **uncountably many** values — if every one carried positive probability, they couldn't possibly sum to $1$; there are too many of them.
    -   So probability gets smeared as a *rate* over the continuum instead of stacked as mass on each point — that rate is the density.
:::

## From Density to Probability {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   $f(x)$ is a **density**, not a probability — it can even be $>1$. Only an *area* under it is a probability.
    -   Compare: a PMF bar height $p(x)$ *is* the probability, directly.
-   To get an actual probability, multiply density by a width: $P(x\le X\le x+dx) \approx f(x)\,dx$.
-   Shrink that width to a single point ($dx\to 0$) and the area vanishes — that's why $P(X=x)=0$ for any one value.
:::

## Notation for the Integral {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   $\displaystyle \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ — the limit of that sum as the strips get infinitely thin.
-   Read $\int$ as "sum" and $dx$ as an infinitesimally thin strip width — the same job as $\Sigma$ and $\Delta x$, just in the limit.
-   $a$ and $b$: where the strips start and stop.
:::

## Anatomy of the Integral {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ has the same three parts as $\displaystyle\sum_{i=a}^{b}$:
    -   $f(x)$ is the **integrand** — what gets summed, same job as $f(x_i)$ inside $\sum_i f(x_i)$.
    -   $dx$ is the **variable of integration** — the infinitesimal step, same job as the index (or $\Delta x$) in $\Sigma$.
    -   $a$ and $b$ are the **limits of integration** — same job as the bounds on $\Sigma$.
:::

## This Is Already Familiar {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   $P(a\le X\le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ — area under the PDF between $a$ and $b$.
-   $E[X] = \int x\,f(x)\,dx$ — same "weight by probability, add up" idea as $\sum_x x\,p(x)$, with $\int$ standing in for $\Sigma$.
-   Day 3 used $\int$ as a symbol; today it's a Riemann-sum limit — a shrinking sum of rectangles, same as $\Sigma$ but with the step size going to zero.
:::

## Quick Drill: Reading $\int$ (1/3) {.smaller}

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.8em;"}
-   Is $\displaystyle\int_1^3 f(x)\,dx$ a number or a function? What about $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx$?
    -   **Answer:** with bounds, a single number — the area from $1$ to $3$. Without bounds, a whole function — it gets a name (the antiderivative) when we solve integrals later today.
-   Given $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, state in words what it represents.
    -   **Answer:** the area under $f$ between $a$ and $b$ — and when $f$ is a PDF, that area is $P(a\le X\le b)$.
:::

## Quick Drill: Reading $\int$ (2/3) {.smaller}

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.8em;"}
-   Discrete CDF: $F(4)=\sum_{k=0}^{4} p(k)$. For a continuous $X$, $F(4)$ becomes…
    -   **(a)** $\sum_{x\le 4} f(x)$
    -   **(b)** $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{4} f(x)\,dx$
    -   **(c)** $f(4)$
    -   **Answer:** (b) — $\Sigma \to \int$, $p(k) \to f(x)\,dx$. (a) can't work: uncountably many points, each with probability $0$. (c) is a density height, not a probability.
-   Discrete mean: $E[X]=\sum_x x\,p(x)$. The continuous version is…
    -   **(a)** $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx$
    -   **(b)** $\displaystyle\int x\,f(x)\,dx$
    -   **(c)** $\displaystyle\int x\,dx$
    -   **Answer:** (b) — same "weight each value, add up" move. (a) is total probability, always $1$. (c) forgets the distribution entirely.
:::

## Quick Drill: Reading $\int$ (3/3) {.smaller}

```{=html}
      <text x="70" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5A6B80">a</text>
      <text x="130" y="136" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5A6B80">b</text>
    </g>
    <g transform="translate(250,0)">
      <path d="M10,120 Q100,-80 190,120 Z" fill="#EDF0F5" stroke="none"/>
      <g clip-path="url(#pdfClipDrillB)">

      </g>
      <path d="M10,120 Q100,-80 190,120" fill="none" stroke="#22303F" stroke-width="2"/>

      <line x1="10" y1="120" x2="190" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5"/>

    </g>
  </g>

```

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.7em;"}
-   **Plot A** — the shaded area is…
    -   **(a)** $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$
    -   **(b)** $f(b)-f(a)$
    -   **(c)** $\int_a^b x\,f(x)\,dx$
    -   **Answer:** (a) — the strip-sum between $a$ and $b$; for a PDF, $P(a\le X\le b)$. (b) is two heights, not an area; (c) is expectation's integrand.
-   **Plot B** — everything shaded from the far left up to $c$ is…
    -   **(a)** $f(c)$
    -   **(b)** $\int_{-\infty}^{c} f(x)\,dx$
    -   **(c)** $\int_{c}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx$
    -   **Answer:** (b) — all probability up to $c$: the CDF $F(c)=P(X\le c)$. (a) is a height (a density); (c) is the *other* tail, $1-F(c)$.
:::

## Limits

*Naming the move we've been leaning on all day: shrink a step to zero, see where things settle.*

## Why We Need It {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   We just shrank a width to zero and trusted the result to settle: rectangles → area. Day 3's bars → curve was the same move, asserted without a name.
    -   "Settles" is doing real work there — some things don't settle at all.
-   Differentiation, coming up, is *defined* as a limit — we can't even write it down without one.
:::

## Getting Arbitrarily Close {.smaller}

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; margin: 4px 0 4px;">
<svg width="470" height="205" viewBox="0 0 470 205" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <text x="235" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303F">xₙ = 1 + 3/n</text>
  <g transform="translate(0,15)">
    <line x1="40" y1="130" x2="440" y2="130" stroke="#B23A48" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5,4"/>
    <text x="44" y="124" font-size="12" fill="#B23A48">L = 1</text>
    <text x="18" y="45" font-size="12" font-style="italic" fill="#22303F">xₙ</text>
    <circle cx="60" cy="10" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="92.7" cy="70" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="125.5" cy="90" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="158.2" cy="100" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="190.9" cy="106" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="223.6" cy="110" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="256.4" cy="112.9" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="289.1" cy="115" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="321.8" cy="116.7" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="354.5" cy="118" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="387.3" cy="119.1" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <circle cx="420" cy="120" r="4.5" fill="#2b6cb0"/>
    <line x1="40" y1="170" x2="440" y2="170" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="60" y="184" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5A6B80">n = 1</text>
    <text x="420" y="184" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5A6B80">n = 12</text>
  </g>
</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.incremental}
-   A **sequence** is an ordered list of numbers: $x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ — here $x_n = 1 + \frac{3}{n}$: $\;4,\; 2.5,\; 2,\; 1.75,\; \dots$
-   The terms never reach $1$, but past any point they stay as close to $1$ as you like — the sequence **converges** to $1$.
-   $\{i\} = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ never settles — it **diverges**.
:::

## Infinite Sums {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   A **series** is the sum of a sequence — the $\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i$ we've used since Day 1, now with $N \to \infty$.
-   $\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^i} = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{4} + \tfrac{1}{8} + \dots = 2$ — infinitely many terms, finite total.
    -   Every PMF fact like $\sum_k p(k) = 1$ over countably many outcomes is this kind of convergent series.
-   $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} i = 1 + 2 + 3 + \dots$ blows up — divergent.
:::

```{=html}
</style>

<script>
(function () {
  var container = document.querySelectorAll('.viz-limit2side');
  container = container[container.length - 1];

  var slider = container.querySelector('#viz-limit2side-slider');
  var deltaReadout = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-delta-readout');
  var curve = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-curve');
  var lguide = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-lguide');
  var rguide = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-rguide');
  var lh = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-lh');
  var rh = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-rh');
  var ldot = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-ldot');
  var rdot = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-rdot');
  var llab = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-llab');
  var rlab = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-rlab');
  var fleftEl = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-fleft');
  var frightEl = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-fright');
  var gapEl = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-gap');
  var verbal = container.querySelector('.viz-limit2side-verbal');

  // Same density as Day 3's PDF/CDF slider: f(x) = 12 x^2 (1-x), Beta(3,2).
  var C = 0.5;
  function xPix(s) { return 60 + 400 * s; }
  function pdfVal(s) { return 12 * s * s * (1 - s); }
  function pdfYPix(v) { return 210 - 90 * v; }

  var d = '';
  for (var i = 0; i <= 100; i++) {
    var s = i / 100;
    d += (i === 0 ? 'M' : 'L') + xPix(s).toFixed(1) + ',' + pdfYPix(pdfVal(s)).toFixed(1);
  }
  curve.setAttribute('d', d);

  function place(guide, hline, dot, lab, x) {
    var px = xPix(x);
    var f = pdfVal(x);
    var py = pdfYPix(f);
    guide.setAttribute('x1', px); guide.setAttribute('x2', px);
    guide.setAttribute('y1', 210); guide.setAttribute('y2', py);
    hline.setAttribute('x2', px); hline.setAttribute('y1', py); hline.setAttribute('y2', py);
    dot.setAttribute('cx', px); dot.setAttribute('cy', py);
    lab.setAttribute('x', px);
    return f;
  }

  function update() {
    var delta = Number(slider.value);
    deltaReadout.textContent = delta.toFixed(3);

    var fl = place(lguide, lh, ldot, llab, C - delta);
    var fr = place(rguide, rh, rdot, rlab, C + delta);

    // Below-axis labels collide with each other and with "c = 0.5" when the
    // dots get close -- fade them out instead of letting them overlap.
    var labVis = delta < 0.06 ? 'hidden' : 'visible';
    llab.setAttribute('visibility', labVis);
    rlab.setAttribute('visibility', labVis);

    fleftEl.textContent = fl.toFixed(3);
    frightEl.textContent = fr.toFixed(3);
    gapEl.textContent = Math.abs(fr - fl).toFixed(3);

    var agree = delta <= 0.01;
    container.classList.toggle('viz-limit2side-agree', agree);
    verbal.textContent = agree
      ? 'Pinned as tight as you like around one number — that number is the limit: f(x) → 1.5 as x → 0.5.'
      : 'Drag δ toward 0 and watch the two heights converge on L.';
  }

  slider.addEventListener('input', update);
  update();
})();
</script>
```

::: {.incremental}
-   Same density you dragged on Day 3. Squeeze $x$ toward $c$ from below (red) and from above (green): the two heights $f(x)$ get pinned as tightly around one number as you like — without ever needing to *arrive* at $c$.
-   That number is what the next slide's notation names: the **limit** of $f$ at $c$.
:::

## Limit Notation {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} x_n = L$ — "as $n$ grows without bound, $x_n$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$."
    -   Converges: a finite limit $L$ exists. Diverges: no limit, or $\pm\infty$.
-   Functions have limits too: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$ — as $x$ steps closer and closer to $c$, $f(x)$ closes in on $L$.
    -   Now $x$ can approach from below or from above: $\lim_{x\to c^-}$ and $\lim_{x\to c^+}$. The limit exists when both sides agree.
-   $f$ doesn't have to be defined *at* $c$ for the limit to exist — only near it. That loophole is about to matter.
:::

```{=html}
.viz-riemannlim-readout { flex: 0 0 auto; display: flex; justify-content: center; gap: 16px; font-size: 0.5em; }
.viz-riemannlim-card {
  background: #F7F8FA; border: 1px solid #EDF0F5; border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 4px 14px; text-align: center; min-width: 130px;
  transition: background 0.3s ease, border-color 0.3s ease;
}
.viz-riemannlim-card-label { display: block; font-size: 0.85em; color: #5A6B80; }
.viz-riemannlim-card-value { display: block; font-size: 1.15em; font-weight: 700; color: #22303F; }
.viz-riemannlim.viz-riemannlim-agree .viz-riemannlim-card { background: #EAF6EF; border-color: #38a169; }
.viz-riemannlim.viz-riemannlim-agree .viz-riemannlim-card-value { color: #2f855a; }
.viz-riemannlim-verbal { flex: 0 0 auto; font-size: 0.5em; font-style: italic; color: #5A6B80; text-align: center; }
.viz-riemannlim.viz-riemannlim-agree .viz-riemannlim-verbal { color: #2f855a; }
</style>

<script>
(function () {
  var container = document.querySelectorAll('.viz-riemannlim');
  container = container[container.length - 1];

  var slider = container.querySelector('#viz-riemannlim-slider');
  var nReadout = container.querySelector('.viz-riemannlim-n-readout');
  var curve = container.querySelector('.viz-riemannlim-curve');
  var rects = container.querySelector('.viz-riemannlim-rects');
  var dxEl = container.querySelector('.viz-riemannlim-dx');
  var sumEl = container.querySelector('.viz-riemannlim-sum');
  var verbal = container.querySelector('.viz-riemannlim-verbal');
  var svgNS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';

  // Same density as the previous slide (and Day 3): f(x) = 12 x^2 (1-x).
  function xPix(s) { return 60 + 400 * s; }
  function pdfVal(s) { return 12 * s * s * (1 - s); }
  function pdfYPix(v) { return 210 - 90 * v; }

  var d = '';
  for (var i = 0; i <= 100; i++) {
    var s = i / 100;
    d += (i === 0 ? 'M' : 'L') + xPix(s).toFixed(1) + ',' + pdfYPix(pdfVal(s)).toFixed(1);
  }
  curve.setAttribute('d', d);

  function update() {
    var n = Number(slider.value);
    var dx = 1 / n;
    nReadout.textContent = n;
    dxEl.textContent = dx.toFixed(3);

    while (rects.firstChild) rects.removeChild(rects.firstChild);

    // Left-endpoint rectangles: height f(i/n), width 1/n.
    var sum = 0;
    for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      var f = pdfVal(i / n);
      sum += f * dx;
      var y = pdfYPix(f);
      var r = document.createElementNS(svgNS, 'rect');
      r.setAttribute('x', xPix(i / n).toFixed(1));
      r.setAttribute('y', y.toFixed(1));
      r.setAttribute('width', (400 / n).toFixed(1));
      r.setAttribute('height', (210 - y).toFixed(1));
      r.setAttribute('fill', '#2b6cb0');
      r.setAttribute('fill-opacity', '0.35');
      r.setAttribute('stroke', '#2b6cb0');
      r.setAttribute('stroke-width', '1');
      rects.appendChild(r);
    }
    sumEl.textContent = sum.toFixed(3);

    var agree = Math.abs(sum - 1) <= 0.01;
    container.classList.toggle('viz-riemannlim-agree', agree);
    verbal.textContent = agree
      ? 'Σ has locked onto the area: the limit of the Riemann sum is ∫₀¹ f(x) dx = 1.'
      : 'Push n up — the staircase melts into the curve.';
  }

  slider.addEventListener('input', update);
  update();
})();
</script>
```

::: {.incremental}
-   Day 3 watched bars melt into a curve; here *you* drive it — every extra rectangle shrinks $\Delta x$, and the staircase sum $\sum_i f(x_i)\,\Delta x$ closes in on the area.
-   The next slide is nothing more than this picture, written down.
:::

## The Riemann-Sum Limit, Formally {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   $\displaystyle \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)\,\Delta x$ — the bars-to-curve picture, written down. The Riemann sum's arrow, cashed in.
-   Every $\Sigma$ from Days 1–2 has this same shape: index, terms, add up. The only new piece is $\Delta x \to 0$.
-   Same move underwrites $E[X]=\sum_x x\,p(x)$ becoming $E[X]=\int x\,f(x)\,dx$ for a continuous $X$.
:::

## Quick Drill: Limits in Context (1/4) {.smaller}

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.8em;"}
-   $\displaystyle\lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \sum_i f(x_i)\,\Delta x$ is…
    -   **(a)** $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$
    -   **(b)** $f'(x)$
    -   **(c)** it diverges — infinitely many terms
    -   **Answer:** (a) — thinner strips, more of them, and the sum settles on the area. Infinitely many terms can still settle: that's convergence.
-   Day 3's binomial bars, with more and more flips and ever-thinner bars: the limiting object is…
    -   **(a)** a CDF $F(x)$
    -   **(b)** a PDF $f(x)$
    -   **(c)** the expected value $E[X]$
    -   **Answer:** (b) — the PMF's bars melt into a density curve. Heights stop being probabilities; areas take over.
:::

## Quick Drill: Limits in Context (2/4) {.smaller}

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; margin: 0;">
<svg width="390" height="130" viewBox="0 0 470 155" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <line x1="30" y1="35" x2="450" y2="35" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4,3"/>
  <text x="24" y="39" text-anchor="end" font-size="12" fill="#5A6B80">1</text>
  <path d="M30,128 C180,127 230,37 450,36" fill="none" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <line x1="30" y1="130" x2="450" y2="130" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="24" y="134" text-anchor="end" font-size="12" fill="#5A6B80">0</text>
  <text x="446" y="148" text-anchor="end" font-size="12" font-style="italic" fill="#5A6B80">x</text>
  <text x="60" y="60" font-size="13" font-style="italic" fill="#22303F">CDF F(x)</text>
</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.7em;"}
-   A CDF $F$, pushed all the way right: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\infty} F(x)$ is…
    -   **(a)** $1$
    -   **(b)** $\infty$
    -   **(c)** depends on the distribution
    -   **Answer:** (a) — $F(x)$ accumulates probability as $x$ grows; in the limit it has accumulated *all* of it, and total probability is $1$ for every distribution.
-   And pushed all the way left: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to-\infty} F(x)$ is…
    -   **(a)** $-1$
    -   **(b)** $0$
    -   **(c)** $f(-\infty)$
    -   **Answer:** (b) — nothing accumulated yet. Every CDF carries these two limits built in: $0$ on the far left, $1$ on the far right.
:::


::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.7em;"}
-   A *discrete* RV's CDF is a staircase. At $x = 1$, does $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 1} F(x)$ exist?
    -   **(a)** yes — it's $0.75$
    -   **(b)** yes — it's $0.25$
    -   **(c)** no — from below $F \to 0.25$, from above $F \to 0.75$
    -   **Answer:** (c) — the one-sided limits disagree, so the two-sided limit doesn't exist. And the jump *is* the PMF: its height, $0.75 - 0.25 = 0.5$, is exactly $P(X=1)$.
:::

## Quick Drill: Limits in Context (4/4) {.smaller}

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.8em;"}
-   A *continuous* RV's CDF has no jumps — both one-sided limits agree everywhere. What does that say about $P(X = x)$ at any exact value?
    -   **(a)** $P(X=x) = f(x)$
    -   **(b)** $P(X=x) = 0$
    -   **(c)** can't tell from the CDF
    -   **Answer:** (b) — the jump height at $x$ is exactly $P(X=x)$; no jump means zero. Day 3's "an exact value has probability $0$" is a statement about limits.
-   For any PMF $p$: $\displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{k=0}^{N} p(k)$ is…
    -   **(a)** $1$
    -   **(b)** $\infty$
    -   **(c)** $0$
    -   **Answer:** (a) — "probabilities sum to $1$" over infinitely many outcomes is a convergent series, like $\sum 1/2^i$ from the Infinite Sums slide.
:::

## Differentiation

*The same shrinking-width limit as Integration, run the other direction.*

## Why We Need It {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   The opening slide's second question is still open: at a particular value of an RV, how fast is the chance changing? A curve's height alone won't answer that — we need its *slope*.
-   Day 1 found $\bar x$ minimizes $\sum(x_i-c)^2$ by algebra alone. Most minimization criteria aren't that friendly — we need a general tool for "where is this function flattest."
:::

## Change We Can Already Measure {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   Across two years, change is a **first difference**: $x_{t+1} - x_t$.
    -   A country's polyarchy score: $0.42$ in 2010 $\to$ $0.45$ in 2011 — first difference $+0.03$.
    -   As a **percentage change**: $\dfrac{x_{t+1}-x_t}{x_t} = \dfrac{0.03}{0.42} \approx +7\%$.
-   Day 3's other running variable already *is* one: **growth** is the percentage first difference of GDP, year over year.
-   Both recipes need **two** snapshots — a year and the year after. Subtract, divide by the gap, done.
-   But ask "how fast was the score changing *in 2010 itself*?" and there's only the 2010 number: nothing to subtract, and a zero-length gap to divide by.
    -   The derivative is the tool that gets an honest answer out of exactly that situation — next slide.
:::

## Secant to Tangent {.smaller}

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; margin: 4px 0 4px;">
<svg width="470" height="210" viewBox="0 0 470 210" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <text x="100" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303F">Secant: two years</text>
  <text x="360" y="14" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#22303F">Tangent: one instant</text>
  <text x="10" y="34" font-size="11" font-style="italic" fill="#22303F">y(t)</text>
  <text x="280" y="34" font-size="11" font-style="italic" fill="#22303F">y(t)</text>
  <g transform="translate(0,20)">
    <line x1="37" y1="69" x2="37" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
    <line x1="100" y1="20" x2="100" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
    <line x1="20" y1="82" x2="120" y2="4" stroke="#B23A48" stroke-width="2"/>
    <path d="M10,120 Q100,-80 190,120" fill="none" stroke="#22303F" stroke-width="2"/>
    <circle cx="37" cy="69" r="4" fill="#B23A48"/>
    <circle cx="100" cy="20" r="4" fill="#B23A48"/>
    <line x1="10" y1="120" x2="190" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="37" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5A6B80">t</text>
    <text x="100" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5A6B80">t + h</text>
    <text x="100" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303F">slope = (y(t+h) − y(t)) / h</text>

    <path d="M212,70 L248,70 M240,63 L248,70 L240,77" fill="none" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="2"/>
    <text x="230" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5A6B80">h → 0</text>

    <g transform="translate(270,0)">
      <line x1="64" y1="36" x2="64" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3,3"/>
      <line x1="12" y1="82" x2="102" y2="2" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="2"/>
      <path d="M10,120 Q100,-80 190,120" fill="none" stroke="#22303F" stroke-width="2"/>
      <circle cx="64" cy="36" r="4" fill="#2f855a"/>
      <line x1="10" y1="120" x2="190" y2="120" stroke="#5A6B80" stroke-width="1.5"/>
      <text x="64" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5A6B80">t</text>
    </g>
    <text x="360" y="152" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#22303F">slope = y′(t)</text>
  </g>
</svg>
</div>
```

::: {.incremental}
-   Let $y(t)$ be the country's polyarchy score over time. A **secant** joins two years, $t$ and $t+h$; its slope, $\dfrac{y(t+h)-y(t)}{h}$, is the average change per year between them.
    -   At $h = 1$ it *is* the last slide's first difference: $y_{2011} - y_{2010}$ over a gap of one.
-   Shrink $h \to 0$: the two years merge and the secant settles into the **tangent** — the score's rate of change *at* the moment $t$. The one-snapshot question, answered.
-   Same $\Delta x \to 0$ move as the Riemann sum, aimed at a slope instead of an area.
:::

```{=html}
}
.viz-sec2tan-card-label { display: block; font-size: 0.85em; color: #5A6B80; }
.viz-sec2tan-card-value { display: block; font-size: 1.15em; font-weight: 700; color: #22303F; }
.viz-sec2tan.viz-sec2tan-agree .viz-sec2tan-card { background: #EAF6EF; border-color: #38a169; }
.viz-sec2tan.viz-sec2tan-agree .viz-sec2tan-card-value { color: #2f855a; }

</style>

<script>
(function () {
  var container = document.querySelectorAll('.viz-sec2tan');
  container = container[container.length - 1];

  var slider = container.querySelector('#viz-sec2tan-slider');
  var hReadout = container.querySelector('.viz-sec2tan-h-readout');
  var curve = container.querySelector('.viz-sec2tan-curve');
  var secant = container.querySelector('.viz-sec2tan-secant');
  var p1 = container.querySelector('.viz-sec2tan-p1');
  var p1lab = container.querySelector('.viz-sec2tan-p1lab');
  var slopeEl = container.querySelector('.viz-sec2tan-slope');
  var verbal = container.querySelector('.viz-sec2tan-verbal');

  // Same density as the earlier viz slides: f(x) = 12 x^2 (1-x).
  // Anchor point x0 = 0.3, where f'(x0) = 12(2x - 3x^2) = 3.96.
  var X0 = 0.3;
  var FPRIME = 3.96;
  function xPix(s) { return 60 + 400 * s; }
  function pdfVal(s) { return 12 * s * s * (1 - s); }
  function pdfYPix(v) { return 210 - 90 * v; }

  var d = '';
  for (var i = 0; i <= 100; i++) {
    var s = i / 100;
    d += (i === 0 ? 'M' : 'L') + xPix(s).toFixed(1) + ',' + pdfYPix(pdfVal(s)).toFixed(1);
  }
  curve.setAttribute('d', d);

  function update() {
    var h = Number(slider.value);
    hReadout.textContent = h.toFixed(3);

    var f0 = pdfVal(X0);
    var f1 = pdfVal(X0 + h);
    var m = (f1 - f0) / h;
    slopeEl.textContent = m.toFixed(3);

    p1.setAttribute('cx', xPix(X0 + h));
    p1.setAttribute('cy', pdfYPix(f1));
    p1lab.setAttribute('x', xPix(X0 + h));
    p1lab.setAttribute('visibility', h < 0.06 ? 'hidden' : 'visible');

    // Draw the secant extended a little past both points (clamped to [0,1]).
    var xa = Math.max(0.02, X0 - 0.15);
    var xb = Math.min(0.98, X0 + h + 0.15);
    secant.setAttribute('x1', xPix(xa));
    secant.setAttribute('y1', pdfYPix(f0 + m * (xa - X0)));
    secant.setAttribute('x2', xPix(xb));
    secant.setAttribute('y2', pdfYPix(f0 + m * (xb - X0)));

    var agree = Math.abs(m - FPRIME) <= 0.05;
    container.classList.toggle('viz-sec2tan-agree', agree);
    verbal.textContent = agree
      ? 'The secant has settled onto the tangent: the limit of the slopes is f′(x) = 3.96.'
      : 'Shrink h — the red secant swings down onto the green tangent.';
  }

  slider.addEventListener('input', update);
  update();
})();
</script>
```

::: {.incremental}
-   Same curve, and the same move as the last two sliders: shrink a gap to zero and watch a number settle. The settling number is the slope *at* $x$.
:::

## Slope, in the Language of Probability {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   The CDF answers "**how much?**": $F(x) = P(X \le x)$ — the probability accumulated by the time you reach $x$.
-   Its slope answers "**how fast?**": how much *new* probability arrives per unit of $x$, right at $x$.
    -   Concretely, Day 3's density: $F(0.50) = 0.313$ and $F(0.51) = 0.328$ — so $0.015$ of probability arrived in a window of width $0.01$.
    -   Rate: $\dfrac{0.328 - 0.313}{0.01} \approx 1.5$ per unit of $x$. Shrink the window and this rate settles — that's a derivative.
-   Steep CDF → probability arriving fast → values near $x$ common. Flat CDF → almost nothing arriving → values near $x$ rare.
-   "Probability per unit of $x$" already has a name: the **density**. Next slide: the CDF's slope *is* $f(x)$, at every $x$.
:::

```{=html}
<script>
(function () {
  var container = document.querySelectorAll('.viz-cdf2pdf');
  container = container[container.length - 1];

  var slider = container.querySelector('#viz-cdf2pdf-slider');
  var xReadout = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-x-readout');
  var cdfCurve = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-cdf-curve');
  var pdfCurve = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-pdf-curve');
  var tan = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-tan');
  var cdfDot = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-cdf-dot');
  var guide = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-guide');
  var pdfDot = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-pdf-dot');
  var slopeReadout = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-slope-readout');
  var heightReadout = container.querySelector('.viz-cdf2pdf-height-readout');

  // Day 3's pair: f(x) = 12 x^2 (1-x), F(x) = 4x^3 - 3x^4, and F'(x) = f(x).
  function xPix(s) { return 60 + 400 * s; }
  function pdfVal(s) { return 12 * s * s * (1 - s); }
  function cdfVal(s) { return 4 * Math.pow(s, 3) - 3 * Math.pow(s, 4); }
  function pdfYPix(v) { return 210 - 90 * v; }
  function cdfYPix(v) { return 210 - 180 * v; }

  var dp = '', dc = '';
  for (var i = 0; i <= 100; i++) {
    var s = i / 100;
    dp += (i === 0 ? 'M' : 'L') + xPix(s).toFixed(1) + ',' + pdfYPix(pdfVal(s)).toFixed(1);
    dc += (i === 0 ? 'M' : 'L') + xPix(s).toFixed(1) + ',' + cdfYPix(cdfVal(s)).toFixed(1);
  }
  pdfCurve.setAttribute('d', dp);
  cdfCurve.setAttribute('d', dc);

  function update() {
    var s = Number(slider.value);
    xReadout.textContent = s.toFixed(2);

    var f = pdfVal(s);
    var px = xPix(s);
    var cy = cdfYPix(cdfVal(s));
    var py = pdfYPix(f);

    // Tangent segment on the CDF: data slope f becomes f * 180/400 in pixels.
    var mPix = f * 180 / 400;
    var dx = 45;
    tan.setAttribute('x1', px - dx); tan.setAttribute('y1', cy + mPix * dx);
    tan.setAttribute('x2', px + dx); tan.setAttribute('y2', cy - mPix * dx);
    cdfDot.setAttribute('cx', px); cdfDot.setAttribute('cy', cy);

    guide.setAttribute('x1', px); guide.setAttribute('x2', px); guide.setAttribute('y2', py);
    pdfDot.setAttribute('cx', px); pdfDot.setAttribute('cy', py);

    slopeReadout.textContent = f.toFixed(3);
    heightReadout.textContent = f.toFixed(3);
  }

  slider.addEventListener('input', update);
  update();
})();
</script>
```

## What a Derivative Is {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   $f'(x) = \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \displaystyle\lim_{h \to 0}\, \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$ — the limit of the secant slope.
-   Read it as the **instantaneous rate of change** of $f$: the slope of the curve at the point $x$.
-   $f'$ is itself a function — a slope at every $x$.
:::

## Quick Drill: Reading $\dfrac{d}{dx}$ (1/3) {.smaller}

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.8em;"}
-   Is $f'(3)$ a number or a function? What about $f'$?
    -   **Answer:** $f'(3)$ is a single number — the slope of $f$ right at $x=3$. $f'$ is a whole function: a slope at every $x$. (Same split as $\int_1^3 f\,dx$ vs. $\int f\,dx$.)
-   $f'(x)$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ — same thing or different things?
    -   **Answer:** the same object, two notations: Lagrange's $f'(x)$ and Leibniz's $\frac{dy}{dx}$ (with $y = f(x)$). Both say: how much $y$ moves per tiny nudge of $x$ — a first difference with the gap shrunk to zero.
    -   You'll meet both in the wild — papers write $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}$-style Leibniz for clarity about *what varies*, $f'$ for brevity.
:::

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.7em;"}
-   At which point is $f'(x) = \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$?
    -   **(a)** A
    -   **(b)** B
    -   **(c)** C
    -   **Answer:** (b) — the tangent at the peak is flat. Hold that thought: "find where the slope is zero" becomes our optimization tool this afternoon.
-   At which point is $f'(x)$ *negative*?
    -   **(a)** A
    -   **(b)** B
    -   **(c)** C
    -   **Answer:** (c) — the curve is falling there, so the rate of change is negative. At A it's rising: $f'(x) > 0$.
:::

## Quick Drill: Reading $\dfrac{d}{dx}$ (3/3) {.smaller}

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.8em;"}
-   For a continuous RV, $F'(x)$ is…
    -   **(a)** $f(x)$
    -   **(b)** $P(X = x)$
    -   **(c)** the area under $f$ up to $x$
    -   **Answer:** (a) — the slider you just dragged: the CDF's slope at $x$ is the density. (b) is $0$ for a continuous RV (last drill!); (c) is $F(x)$ itself, not its slope.
-   Where the CDF is at its *steepest*, the PDF is…
    -   **(a)** at its peak
    -   **(b)** zero
    -   **(c)** equal to $1$
    -   **Answer:** (a) — steepest accumulation = highest density. And where the CDF has gone flat, $f(x) = 0$: no probability arriving.
:::

## Trivia: Pebbles and a Stretched S {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
-   **"Calculus" is Latin for "small pebble"** — the counting stones of a Roman abacus. Medicine still uses the old sense: kidney stones are *renal calculi*.
    -   Newton called his version "the method of fluxions"; Leibniz's names — *calculus differentialis* and *calculus integralis* — are the ones that stuck.
-   **The $\int$ is a stretched S.** Leibniz introduced it in a 1675 manuscript by elongating the long s (ſ) of Latin *summa* — "sum."
    -   The notation itself remembers what we built this morning: an integral *is* a sum of thin strips.
-   Sources: [History of calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_calculus) · [Integral symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_symbol)
:::
